blocks.html: Every breeding candidate undergoes extensive health testing, including hip and elbow certification, comprehensive DNA screening, and a full veterinary examination. I only breed dogs that meet my strict health and working requirements — health testing is a baseline, not the whole picture.

Breeding decisions go beyond a health clearance and a good pedigree on paper. I look for genuine complementary drive character between sire and dam — lines that fill in each other's gaps rather than stacking the same strengths and the same risks. I also work closely with the math behind it: coefficient-of-inbreeding calculations across the full pedigree, not just the first two or three generations, so I understand exactly what I'm concentrating and what I'm diluting before a breeding decision is made.

I've also brought in outside lines deliberately — including dogs from rare, closed Belgian working bloodlines used by special forces and law enforcement programs — specifically to strengthen genetic depth rather than simply chase a name on paper. It's a slower way to breed and develop dogs, but it gives me more control over what I'm producing and why each pairing is made.

I keep the breeding program small and selective. The goal is not to produce more litters — it's to give the training program better raw material to work with. A pedigree tells you what's possible in a dog. It doesn't tell you what's actually there. I still have to evaluate every dog directly, and that's the part no amount of pedigree research replaces.
